name: Chiari Malformation Type I

criteria.description: Cerebellar tonsillar herniation >5mm below the foramen magnum on sagittal MRI
Compatible clinical symptoms (occipital headache, neurological deficits)
Tonsillar herniation 3-5mm with associated syringomyelia or CSF flow obstruction
Abnormal CSF flow dynamics on cine MRI at craniovertebral junction

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Tonsillar herniation >5mm on MRI. 3-5mm herniation may be significant if symptomatic with supportive findings. Clinical correlation essential as many cases are asymptomatic.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Chiari type II involves myelomeningocele and is typically diagnosed in infancy. Chiari 0.5 or Chiari 0 may have symptoms without meeting 5mm threshold.

pathognomonic.notes: Suboccipital headache provoked by coughing, straining, sneezing, or exertion; most characteristic symptom
Dissociated sensory loss (loss of pain/temperature with preserved touch) in a cape distribution
Downbeating nystagmus worse on lateral and downward gaze; characteristic of craniovertebral junction pathology

occasional.notes: Central sleep apnea from brainstem compression
May be presenting sign, especially in children

laboratory: CSF studies if lumbar puncture performed (usually not indicated; risk of tonsillar herniation)
imaging: Sagittal MRI showing cerebellar tonsillar herniation >5mm below foramen magnum
Cine MRI showing altered CSF flow at craniovertebral junction
Basilar invagination or atlantoaxial instability (associated conditions)
MRI entire spine to evaluate for syrinx
genetic: Some familial clustering suggesting genetic predisposition
Associated with connective tissue disorders (Ehlers-Danlos syndrome)
No single causative gene identified for typical CM-I
other: Sleep study to evaluate for central sleep apnea
Brainstem auditory evoked potentials may be abnormal
Somatosensory evoked potentials may show cervical cord dysfunction

distinguishingFeatures: IIH has papilledema and elevated opening pressure
IIH may cause secondary tonsillar herniation
IIH responds to CSF pressure lowering
MS has demyelinating lesions on brain MRI
MS has oligoclonal bands in CSF
MS has dissemination in time and space
Cervical spondylosis shows disc/osteophyte compression on MRI

redFlags: Progressive neurological deficits (myelopathy, brainstem dysfunction) warrant surgical evaluation
Central sleep apnea requires polysomnography and may indicate brainstem compression
Growing syringomyelia indicates ongoing CSF flow obstruction
Scoliosis in children should prompt MRI to evaluate for Chiari/syrinx
Lumbar puncture should generally be avoided without prior imaging due to herniation risk
Associated Ehlers-Danlos syndrome or craniocervical instability may complicate surgical planning
references: Milhorat TH, et al. Chiari I malformation redefined: clinical and radiographic findings for 364 symptomatic patients. Neurosurgery. 1999;44(5):1005-1017.
Arnautovic A, et al. Chiari malformation Type I: a comprehensive review. Neurosurg Focus. 2015;38(4):E2.
Langridge B, et al. Chiari malformation type 1: A systematic review of natural history and conservative management. World Neurosurg. 2017;104:213-219.
